units.title: Unit 57 — Deciding and choosing
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 118–119 (PDF pages 122–123).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Form and qualify decisions with make, take, arrive at, come to and put off, recognising register differences.
Describe doubt, indecision and informed judgement with slight hesitation, second thoughts and reserve judgement.
Discuss difficult choices and opportunities using natural phrases for advice, preference and options.
Distinguish passing up an opportunity, taking the soft option and rejecting a proposal out of hand.

items.example: We need to make a decision before the supplier confirms the order.
items.note: Make is the usual verb with decision; do a decision is incorrect.

items.pt: uma decisão importante; uma decisão de grande impacto
items.example: Choosing a university is a big decision for many young adults.
items.note: Big emphasises the importance or consequences of a decision.

items.pt: adiar a tomada de uma decisão
items.example: You cannot put off making a decision about the lease indefinitely.
items.note: Put off takes an -ing form when followed by an action: put off deciding or put off making a decision.

items.example: I could detect a slight hesitation in her answer to the proposal.
items.note: Detect is often used when someone notices subtle uncertainty in speech or behaviour.

items.pt: reconsiderar; começar a ter dúvidas sobre uma decisão
items.example: After accepting the position, he began to have second thoughts about relocating.
items.note: Having second thoughts means reconsidering a choice already made or almost made.

items.example: The board will take the decision after reviewing the risks.
items.note: A formal, particularly British alternative to make a decision; the two do not always have identical register.

items.example: The committee reached a unanimous decision after reviewing the evidence.
items.note: Unanimous means that everyone entitled to decide agreed on the outcome.

items.example: There is still a degree of uncertainty about the delivery date.
items.note: A degree of softens the statement: the situation is not completely certain.

items.pt: uma decisão sensata; uma decisão acertada
items.example: Bringing backup equipment was a wise decision.
items.note: Wise describes a choice showing good judgement and consideration of future consequences.

items.example: After several interviews, the panel managed to arrive at a decision.
items.note: Arrive at emphasises reaching a decision after thought or discussion.

items.pt: uma decisão sensata; uma decisão prudente
items.example: Keeping some savings aside seems a sensible decision.
items.note: Sensible focuses on practical reasoning rather than excitement or ambition.

items.example: Her sound judgement helped the team avoid an expensive mistake.
items.note: Sound means reliable and well founded here, not related to hearing or noise.

items.pt: defender uma decisão; justificar uma decisão
items.example: The manager had to defend a decision that some employees disliked.
items.note: Defend a decision means give reasons in support of it, especially when criticised.

items.pt: adiar a avaliação; não emitir juízo por enquanto
items.example: I will reserve judgement until the full test results are available.
items.note: Formal expression meaning deliberately wait for more information before forming an opinion.

items.example: It is easier to make a choice when you know your priorities.
items.note: Use make a choice, not do a choice.

items.pt: receber a oportunidade; ter a chance
items.example: She was delighted to be given the chance to lead the new project.
items.note: The expression often introduces an opportunity to do something.

items.example: Winning the scholarship was the opportunity of a lifetime for her.
items.note: Emphatic expression for an exceptionally valuable or rare opportunity.

items.example: He has a burning desire to work in scientific research.
items.note: Burning expresses exceptionally strong motivation or longing.

items.example: I would much prefer to discuss the details in person.
items.note: Much strengthens prefer; would much prefer is natural for a hypothetical or polite preference.

items.example: Before buying the equipment, we should consider all the options.
items.note: Consider means examine possibilities carefully, not merely mention them.

items.example: If you take my advice, you will ask for a written quotation.
items.note: Take someone's advice means follow it, rather than simply hear it.

items.example: I strongly advise you to check the contract before signing.
items.note: Strongly advise commonly introduces the person advised and an infinitive with to.

items.example: We have a choice between repairing the system and replacing it.
items.note: Having a choice means alternatives are available.

items.example: With the laboratory closed, we had no option but to postpone the tests.
items.note: Often followed by but to plus an infinitive: have no option but to leave.

items.example: It was a tough choice between two attractive job offers.
items.note: Tough highlights that choosing is emotionally or practically difficult.

items.example: He took the soft option and avoided the difficult conversation.
items.note: Often mildly critical: the person chooses an easier path rather than a more demanding one.

items.example: She did not want to pass up the opportunity to study abroad.
items.note: Pass up means decide not to use an available chance, sometimes with regret.

items.example: Small businesses often face difficult choices during a recession.
items.note: Face means confront an unavoidable situation, not simply look at it.

items.word: reject an offer out of hand
items.pt: rejeitar uma oferta sem nem considerar
items.example: I would not reject an offer out of hand without reading its terms.
items.note: Out of hand means immediately and without serious consideration.

items.pt: ponderar as opções; avaliar as alternativas
items.example: We need to weigh up the options before selecting a supplier.
items.note: British English phrasal verb for comparing the advantages and disadvantages.

items.example: I hope we can come to a decision during tomorrow's meeting.
items.note: Come to a decision stresses reaching a conclusion, like arrive at a decision.

items.example: Please give me the chance to explain why the prototype failed.
items.note: Give someone the chance is followed naturally by to plus an infinitive.

units.title: Unit 58 — Claiming and denying
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 120–121 (PDF pages 124–125).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise expressions for accusations, hints, disputed claims and public statements without equating allegations with proven facts.
Present and support viewpoints using put forward, back up, make the point and substantiate.
Differentiate deny, reject and refuse according to the noun or complement they take.
Use deny with an -ing clause, refuse with a to-infinitive, and describe contradictory evidence precisely.

items.pt: enfrentar acusações; ser alvo de acusações
items.example: The contractor may face accusations of ignoring safety procedures.
items.note: Face accusations is neutral about whether the allegations are true; often followed by of plus an -ing form.

items.example: Investigators suspected that several officials had agreed to take bribes.
items.note: Take bribes means accept illicit payments; an accusation is not proof of wrongdoing.

items.example: Her colleagues dropped heavy hints about the planned farewell party.
items.note: Heavy hints are strong indirect suggestions; drop heavy hints is a common verb pairing.

items.pt: dar a entender claramente; insinuar de forma clara
items.example: The report seems to clearly imply that the figures were manipulated.
items.note: Imply means suggest without directly stating; the inference should be supported by context.

items.example: The customer kept trying to drop broad hints about wanting a discount.
items.note: Broad hints are easy-to-notice indirect suggestions.

items.example: A leaked document raised questions about the proposed merger.
items.note: Leaked describes information or a document made public without authorisation.

items.example: The article appeared to make serious allegations about the firm's accounts.
items.note: An allegation is a claim of misconduct, not an established fact.

items.example: During the hearing, the witness chose to openly accuse the official of fraud.
items.note: Accuse someone of something; openly means publicly or without concealment.

items.pt: divulgar uma declaração; emitir uma nota oficial
items.example: The university will issue a statement after the investigation ends.
items.note: Issue is formal and common for public or official statements.

items.example: The company described the reports as unfounded claims.
items.note: Unfounded means not supported by evidence; do not automatically treat disputed claims as false.

items.example: The student said she had been wrongly accused of cheating.
items.note: Wrongly accused expresses that an accusation is mistaken or unjustified.

items.pt: uma disputa de longa duração; uma longa batalha
items.example: The two firms remain involved in a long-running battle over licensing fees.
items.note: Battle can be figurative and means an extended conflict or dispute.

items.example: He kept dropping heavy hints that he wanted to leave early.
items.note: The verb drop is conventional with hints; heavy stresses the strength of the implication.

items.pt: apresentar uma teoria; propor uma teoria
items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: The researcher plans to put forward a theory about the observed behaviour.
items.note: Put forward introduces an idea for consideration, not proof that it is correct.

items.pt: fundamentar um argumento; sustentar um argumento
items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: Use reliable measurements to back up an argument in the report.
items.note: Back up means support with reasons or evidence, not merely repeat.

items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: I fully accept that our first estimate was inaccurate.
items.note: Fully expresses complete acceptance of a fact or argument.

items.pt: ressaltar que; apresentar o argumento de que
items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: I want to make the point that accuracy matters more than speed here.
items.note: Introduces a specific assertion or argument rather than merely speaking.

items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: It is widely acknowledged that good documentation reduces maintenance costs.
items.note: Usually used for facts, opinions or contributions recognised by many people.

items.pt: afirmar claramente; declarar de forma explícita
items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: The policy should state clearly who is responsible for each task.
items.note: State clearly emphasises direct and unambiguous communication.

items.pt: fundamentar uma alegação; comprovar uma afirmação
items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: Independent test results will help substantiate a claim about performance.
items.note: Substantiate is formal and means provide evidence in support of a claim.

items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: The author chose to reject earlier ideas after examining new evidence.
items.note: Reject means decide an idea is not acceptable or convincing; it differs from denying an allegation.

items.pt: apresentar um argumento; destacar um ponto
items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: She managed to make a point that changed how we viewed the problem.
items.note: A shorter pattern than make the point that, used for advancing an argument.

items.section: B · Putting forward a point of view
items.example: The latest experiment may help back up a theory proposed last year.
items.note: Back up requires evidence or reasons; the exercise uses it for research-based support.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The director continues to strongly deny any involvement in the scheme.
items.note: Strongly intensifies deny and does not mean that the allegation has been disproved.

items.pt: negar as acusações; contestar as imputações
items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The defendant will deny the charges at the hearing.
items.note: Charges are formal legal allegations; deny takes a direct object.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: She chose to deny an accusation that she had copied the report.
items.note: Deny is appropriate for saying an accusation is untrue.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The singer decided to deny a rumour about his retirement.
items.note: A rumour is unconfirmed information; deny means say it is untrue.

items.pt: negar uma alegação; contestar uma acusação
items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The company issued a letter to deny an allegation of misconduct.
items.note: Use deny with allegations, including those that have not been proven.

items.pt: eximir-se de responsabilidade; declarar que não assume responsabilidade
items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The notice says the operator may disclaim responsibility for unattended belongings.
items.note: Formal, especially legal or contractual; a disclaimer may not remove legal duties.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: We should not reject an idea simply because it comes from a junior engineer.
items.note: Reject an idea means refuse to accept the proposal, not claim that it never existed.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The client may reject a suggestion that increases the cost.
items.note: Reject naturally pairs with suggestions; deny a suggestion is not the usual choice.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: These observations run contrary to the original hypothesis.
items.note: Run contrary to means conflict with facts, expectations, beliefs or another position.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The investigators found contradictory evidence in the two reports.
items.note: Evidence is contradictory when pieces point towards incompatible conclusions.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: I received contradictory advice from two consultants about the same issue.
items.note: Used when different recommendations cannot easily be followed together.

items.pt: negar uma alegação; contestar uma afirmação
items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The spokesperson was quick to deny a claim about the company's finances.
items.note: Deny means assert that a reported claim is not true.

items.pt: rejeitar uma alegação; não aceitar uma afirmação
items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The panel decided to reject a claim that lacked supporting data.
items.note: Reject can mean refuse to accept a claim; deny is also possible but stresses saying it is untrue.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: I had to refuse an invitation because I was already travelling that day.
items.note: Refuse is natural with invitations; deny an invitation is inappropriate for declining it.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: She decided to refuse an offer that did not meet her requirements.
items.note: Use refuse rather than deny for declining an offer; reject an offer can also be natural.

items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: A witness may refuse to cooperate without legal advice.
items.note: Refuse to do something takes a to-infinitive; deny doing something normally looks back to an act.

items.pt: negar ter participado; negar estar envolvido
items.section: C · Denying and responding to claims
items.example: The employee continued to deny being involved in the incident.
items.note: Deny is followed by an -ing clause for an action or involvement being denied.
